meta.description: No — this isn’t a Steve Jobs original. The “richest man in the cemetery” quip traces to comedian Ed Wynn in 1932, decades before Jobs echoed it.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'I don't want to be the richest man in the cemetery'?
meta.ogDescription: Not coined by Steve Jobs. Quote Investigator traces the ‘richest man in the cemetery’ line to comedian Ed Wynn, attested in 1932.

answer.label: Not Steve Jobs — a 1930s quip popularized by Ed Wynn
answer.sourceLine: The “richest man in the cemetery” expression was already in circulation by the 1930s. Quote Investigator found its earliest instance in a January 1932 Boston Globe piece on comedian Ed Wynn. Steve Jobs did voice a version — “Being the richest man in the cemetery doesn’t matter to me” — in a 1993 Wall Street Journal interview, but he was echoing a decades-old saying, not the exact wording popularly pinned on him.

source.excerpt: Boston Globe headline, 1932: “Ed Wynn Doesn’t Yearn to Be Wealthiest Man in Cemetery.” Steve Jobs, WSJ 1993: “Being the richest man in the cemetery doesn’t matter to me … Going to bed at night saying we’ve done something wonderful … that’s what matters to me.”
trail: The definitive tracing is Quote Investigator’s 2011 study, which dates the expression to a January 1932 Boston Globe article about comedian Ed Wynn.

Per the same study, Wynn’s own phrasing was “I have no ambition to be the wealthiest man in the cemetery,” and later users included Douglas MacLean, Clifford Odets, Skeets Gallagher and Colonel Harland Sanders.

Steve Jobs’s documented use — “Being the richest man in the cemetery doesn’t matter to me” — appears in a 1993 Wall Street Journal interview cited by Quote Investigator, decades after the phrase was established.
Aggregators such as Goodreads attach the Jobs version to his name with no note that the underlying quip predates him by sixty years.
source.excerptNote: The exact popular wording is a floating, proverb-like quip rather than a verbatim line from any single person; Wynn’s and Jobs’s documented phrasings both differ from it.

source.rightsNote: The exact popular wording is a proverbial quip with no single identifiable author — it circulated widely from the 1930s onward, so no clean public-domain source can be tied to it. Ed Wynn’s 1932 phrasing was reported in the Boston Globe, and Steve Jobs’s distinct 1993 wording appeared in the Wall Street Journal (in copyright); neither matches the popular line verbatim.

author.name: Ed Wynn
author.heading: Ed Wynn
author.bio: Ed Wynn was a vaudeville, radio and film comedian famous as “The Perfect Fool,” whose fluttery voice and self-deprecating one-liners made him a household name in the 1920s and 1930s. Quote Investigator credits his 1932 quip — “I have no ambition to be the wealthiest man in the cemetery” — as the earliest documented form of the saying. He later won an Emmy and earned an Oscar nomination for The Diary of Anne Frank (1959).

misattribution.heading: Why it gets pinned on Steve Jobs
misattribution.intro: The line rides on Steve Jobs’s anti-materialist mystique, but it is a 1930s show-business quip he merely echoed — and even his own wording differs from the version that circulates.

items.why: Jobs said a related line — “Being the richest man in the cemetery doesn’t matter to me” — in a 1993 Wall Street Journal interview, but the expression predated him by about sixty years.
Quote Investigator found the earliest instance in a January 1932 Boston Globe article, headlined “Ed Wynn Doesn’t Yearn to Be Wealthiest Man in Cemetery.”
The same study lists Douglas MacLean, Clifford Odets, Skeets Gallagher and Colonel Harland Sanders among the many who used the quip in the decades between Wynn and Jobs.

misattribution.truthLine: It’s a decades-old show-business quip — first documented for comedian Ed Wynn in 1932 — not a Steve Jobs original.

context.heading: A quip with a long pedigree
lead: The sentiment — that a fortune buys you nothing once you’re dead — is old folk wisdom, and phrasing it around a cemetery made it a durable comic line. Ed Wynn used it to poke fun at his own success; later entertainers and businessmen reached for it to signal that work, not wealth, was the point.

Steve Jobs’s 1993 version fit his carefully cultivated image of a founder driven by craft rather than money, which is why the internet later collapsed the whole tradition into a single Jobs ‘quote.’ The tidy attribution erases Wynn and everyone in between.
context.detailsSummary: More on the chain of users
detailsBody: Quote Investigator records the phrase passing through silent-film star Douglas MacLean, playwright Clifford Odets, actor Skeets Gallagher and KFC founder Colonel Harland Sanders, and notes it even surfaced in a 1948 song title per Billboard — a spread that long predates Jobs’s use.
context.pull: First documented for a vaudeville comedian in 1932 — not an Apple boardroom.
